chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Abdul Malik al-Qummi, who said:

I and my brother Idris were in the presence of Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him). Idris said, 'May we be sacrificed for you, what is al-maysir (gambling)?' Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) said, 'It is chess (al-shatranj).' I said, 'But people say it is backgammon (al-nard).' He (peace be upon him) said, 'And backgammon as well.'

key_terms.أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: Abu Abdullah; referring to Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him)
key_terms.الشِّطْرَنْجُ: Chess; a strategic board game identified here as gambling
key_terms.النَّرْدُ: Backgammon; a dice-based game also classified as gambling
key_terms.الْمَيْسِرُ: Gambling; specifically games of chance involving stakes

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on chess and backgammon according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: In this concise narration from *Al-Kafi*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the juristic classification of chess (*al-shatranj*) and backgammon (*al-nard*) as forms of *al-maysir* (gambling), addressing contemporary scholarly debates regarding their specific nature. This hadith is pivotal in Shia fiqh for establishing the prohibition of these games, linking them to the broader concept of gambling which entails uncertainty and potential loss of wealth. The confirmation of both games under the same ruling underscores their shared characteristic of being games of chance rather than pure skill, a distinction often debated by jurists.
